title: The "Quick Polish" Request
body: Your PM pings you a Figma link: "quick feedback?" It's 47 screens of AI-generated UI with 11 typefaces. One is Papyrus. Another is also Papyrus, but bold. His only comment says "vibe check: yes?" He made this during a flight delay.

choices.title: Fix what you can, log the hours
choices.body: You spend nine hours fixing someone else's Midjourney fever dream. Sprint velocity says you did nothing.

choices.title: Send a real estimate and watch him pivot
choices.body: You estimate three sprints. He says "wow ok" and asks engineering to just ship it as-is.

choices.title: Screenshot it to the design Slack, no caption
choices.body: The screenshot circulates for three days. Someone makes it their profile pic. The PM finds out. Worth it.

title: Dribbble Likes Are Not Promotions
body: Your side project rebrand gets 847 likes and one comment: "inspo." Your manager does not accept Dribbble likes as evidence of impact. A Canva template made in forty minutes got 2,100 likes yesterday. It used the gradient pack. You know which one.

choices.title: Chase the algorithm, post shallow work
choices.body: You start making glossy throwaway shots. The likes come faster. The work means less.

choices.title: Log off and do real work
choices.body: You close Dribbble and open your actual sprint board. The silence is deafening and then it isn't.

choices.title: DM the Canva person, swallow pride
choices.body: They're actually nice. They teach you engagement hooks. You teach them type hierarchy. Unlikely alliance.

title: Portfolio Update Paralysis
body: Your portfolio hasn't been updated since you joined the company. Everything is under NDA. Every Sunday you open Framer, move one text block two pixels left, and close it. You have 22 projects in a folder called "to add eventually." The folder is from 2024.

choices.title: Block the weekend, ship imperfect
choices.body: You publish the damn thing at 11pm Sunday. It's not perfect. Nothing is. A recruiter reaches out Monday.

choices.title: Ask a design friend to help organize
choices.body: You pay someone in coffee and favors to do the thing you couldn't make yourself do. It works.

choices.title: Send the 2023 link, accept the anxiety
choices.body: It's fine. The work is good. The dates are lies everyone tells.

title: Midjourney Stole Your Aesthetic
body: The marketing team just posted the new campaign on LinkedIn. It looks exactly like the brand system you spent six months on, which they never used. The art direction is clearly Midjourney. The CMO says they "co-created with AI."

choices.title: Write a subtle callout in Slack
choices.body: You hint without naming names in the design channel. The discourse is exhausting but validating.

choices.title: Document everything, escalate to your VP
choices.body: Your VP reads your doc. It costs political capital and feels like punching fog.

choices.title: Channel rage into new work
choices.body: You redesign the component library in three days. Fury is an underrated creative fuel.

title: Make the Logo Bigger
body: The VP of Marketing replies to your final brand presentation: "Can we make the logo bigger?" It is already at the maximum size supported by the nav bar. The logo cannot become bigger without ceasing to be a logo and becoming the entire header.

choices.title: Make it bigger, log the revision
choices.body: You make it bigger. You log the revision in Jira. The logo is now a philosophical statement about corporate identity.

choices.title: Schedule a call, explain visual hierarchy
choices.body: You explain hierarchy for the fourth time. They nod. They understand. They still want it bigger.

choices.title: Add a sarcastic APPROVED stamp, never send
choices.body: You screenshot it and close the file. The satisfaction is private and absolute.

title: The LinkedIn Design Futurist
body: A designer with 34k followers posts "I replaced my entire workflow with AI in 30 days." 4,200 reposts. Your PM sends it to you with a thumbs-up emoji. His bio says "Design Futurist." He went to the same bootcamp. You went to art school for four years.

choices.title: Write your own carousel, begrudgingly
choices.body: You make a carousel about AI in product design. It gets traction. You feel dirty and seen simultaneously.

choices.title: Quietly mute, focus on shipping features
choices.body: You mute him and ship two features that week. Shipped product beats thought leadership.

choices.title: Start a newsletter instead
choices.body: Design Twitter is dead anyway. You write something real. Seven people subscribe. One of them emails back.

title: The Company Hackathon Trap
body: Leadership announces a 48-hour hackathon. Winner gets "visibility with the exec team" and a $50 gift card. The last hackathon winner got promoted. The last three losers got laid off two months later.

choices.title: Skip it and protect your sprint work
choices.body: You decline and ship your tickets on time. Nobody mentions the hackathon to you again.

choices.title: Join a team and build something real
choices.body: You team up with two engineers. The prototype is beautiful. The gift card is $50. The visibility is real.

choices.title: Go all in, design the winning pitch
choices.body: You deliver a pitch deck so clean the CEO asks if it's real. It's not, but the promotion conversation starts.

title: The PM Who Discovered Midjourney
body: Your PM sends a cheerful Slack message. He's started using Midjourney for mockups and "honestly it's been great!" He wants to scale back design involvement to "just the big stuff." He's made a feature mockup with drop shadows on every element.

choices.title: Reposition as strategic design lead
choices.body: You rebrand yourself internally as a design strategist overnight. The scope goes up. The imposter syndrome arrives on schedule.

choices.title: Accept reduced scope, fill time with systems work
choices.body: You take the hit and spend the freed hours on the design system. The long game plays out slowly.

choices.title: Escalate to your design lead
choices.body: Oh wait. You ARE the design lead now. The team used to be six people.

title: Lost the Headcount to AI
body: Your request for a junior designer got denied. The VP shows you a demo of an AI design tool that "replaces the need for additional headcount." The tool generates 40 screens in three minutes. They're all wrong in ways nobody in the room can see.

choices.title: Learn the AI pipeline, prove you're adaptable
choices.body: You spend a weekend learning the tools. You can now do in hours what took days. It feels like winning and losing simultaneously.

choices.title: Double down on what AI can't do
choices.body: User research, stakeholder alignment, systems thinking. The list is shorter than you'd like.

choices.title: Start consulting other teams on AI design workflows
choices.body: You become the internal expert who teaches other teams to use AI. The irony is thick. The visibility is real.

title: The Recruiter That Actually Has a Role
body: You get 20 LinkedIn messages a week. One person replies with a real role. They want a senior product designer. They say "hop on a quick call" and it isn't code for anything terrible. Hope arrives like caffeine.

choices.title: Respond fast with a crisp deck
choices.body: You send a beautiful portfolio deck in 90 minutes. They schedule an onsite. You stare at the calendar invite like it's a love letter.

choices.title: Ask your network about the company first
choices.body: A friend knows the VP of Design. "Great culture but they just cut the team by half." Intel is worth more than speed.

choices.title: Overthink it and let the thread die
choices.body: You draft four replies, send none, and the window closes. Perfectionism is an expensive hobby.

title: The Unpaid Design Review
body: A PM from another team asks for a 45-minute "brainstorm" on their feature. Unpaid by your sprint. They say: "It'll be fun." They also say: "We move fast." You hear: "We don't pay for design thinking."

choices.title: Take the meeting, be generous, hope
choices.body: You give away $500 worth of strategic thinking. They say "amazing, let's circle back." The circle never completes.

choices.title: Require it go through your manager first
choices.body: You say your bandwidth is allocated and CC your lead. The work starts on real footing.

choices.title: Decline politely, protect your sprint
choices.body: You send a template reply and close the tab. Boundaries are a muscle and you just did a rep.

title: The Missing Design Process
body: You realize the team has no design review process. Engineers ship directly from Figma, interpreting your mocks with creative liberty. A button radius changed from 8px to 16px somewhere between design and production. Nobody noticed except you.

choices.title: Write a process doc, require design sign-off
choices.body: You send a professional process proposal. Engineering signs without complaint. You wonder why you were afraid.

choices.title: Pair with engineering, build trust first
choices.body: You frame it as "collaboration improvement." They appreciate the approach.

choices.title: Say nothing, hope they check the specs
choices.body: They don't check the specs. You knew they wouldn't.

title: The Offshore Design Team
body: Leadership hired an offshore design agency for "overflow work" at a quarter of your cost. The agency portfolio is AI-generated. The reviews are five stars. The delivery time is "24 hours." You cannot compete with someone who doesn't sleep because they're in a different timezone.

choices.title: Show the quality gap with real examples
choices.body: You put together a three-minute Loom comparing AI output to your strategic work. Your VP watches 45 seconds and says "noted."

choices.title: Offer to QA the offshore work
choices.body: You become the quality gate. Two hours a day fixing someone else's output. Your title doesn't change.

choices.title: Focus on work they can't offshore
choices.body: Research, strategy, stakeholder alignment. The stuff that requires being in the room.

title: Scope Creep: The Monster Returns
body: The project was a settings page redesign. Then settings and onboarding. Then "while you're at it, can you do the dashboard?" The sprint hasn't changed. The scope has tripled.

choices.title: Push back in standup, reset expectations
choices.body: You bring up scope in the retro. The PM is surprised there are boundaries.

choices.title: Do it all, silently resent everything
choices.body: You deliver the settings, the onboarding, the dashboard, and a piece of your soul.

choices.title: Propose a phased approach in the roadmap
choices.body: You break the work into three milestones with three timelines. Organization is design too.

title: The Design Conference Spiral
body: The company sends you to a design conference. Everyone's bio says "Head of" or "VP." Yours says "Senior Product Designer." You spend the first keynote wondering if you belong here. The team used to send three designers. Now it's just you.

choices.title: Talk to strangers, network aggressively
choices.body: You introduce yourself to 15 people. Three exchange numbers. One becomes a lifeline six months later.

choices.title: Attend workshops, learn something real
choices.body: You skip networking and attend three hands-on sessions. You learn more in four hours than in four months of Figma Community.

choices.title: Leave at lunch, save what's left of you
choices.body: You grab a free tote bag that says CREATE FEARLESSLY in Futura Bold. You create anxiously at your standing desk.

title: Design Awards Are Dead
body: You pitch submitting the redesign to three design awards. Your manager asks for the ROI. You say "brand credibility." They say "can you put that in a spreadsheet?" You can't. Your ego has a subscription model but the company won't expense it.

choices.title: Submit on your own dime, play the prestige game
choices.body: You win one. Bronze. The trophy costs more than the award is worth to anyone. Your manager doesn't mention it.

choices.title: Skip awards, write a case study instead
choices.body: You take the energy and write a detailed case study for your portfolio. More eyeballs than any jury.

choices.title: Let it go, awards don't survive reorgs
choices.body: You close the tab. Nobody at your company has ever mentioned a design award in a performance review.

title: Project Canceled Mid-Sprint
body: You're three weeks into a feature redesign. You present the midpoint to stakeholders. The project gets deprioritized. Not because the work is bad. Because the roadmap shifted. Your Figma file joins the graveyard of canceled initiatives.

choices.title: Document the work for future reference
choices.body: You write up the rationale and archive the designs. Six months later, a new PM finds it and ships it.

choices.title: Post the work on Dribbble as a concept
choices.body: You publish the work as a concept study. It's some of your best stuff. The PM never notices.

choices.title: Move on immediately, don't look back
choices.body: You close the file, label it canceled_q3_v2, and open the next ticket.

title: The Portfolio You're Ashamed Of
body: A recruiter asks for your portfolio link. You send it and immediately think of six things wrong with it. The case studies are old. Half the products have pivoted. The about page photo is from 2022 when your team still existed.

choices.title: Follow up with a personal note to contextualize
choices.body: You email: "Some of this is dated but here's what I'm working on now." They appreciate the honesty.

choices.title: Speed-update the worst parts overnight
choices.body: You fix the mobile bug, swap two case studies, and update the photo at midnight.

choices.title: Send it and stop thinking about it
choices.body: You hit send and close the tab. The work is the work.

title: The Blockchain Feature Request
body: The CEO comes back from a conference and says: "Have you thought about adding web3 integration to the product?" It's 2026. You search their face for irony. There is none. They watched a YouTube video on the plane.

choices.title: Explain gently why this isn't a product strategy
choices.body: You redirect to actual growth tactics. They nod. They mention blockchain one more time. Then never again.

choices.title: Design the exploration, bill the sprint
choices.body: You spend a sprint exploring web3 UX. The mocks are beautiful. They never mention it again.

choices.title: Refuse and risk looking resistant
choices.body: You say no. They look at you like you don't understand the future. Your PM backs you up eventually.

title: The Critique Group
body: A designer from another company invites you to a private critique group. Six designers, all in-house, all the last designer on their team. Monthly sessions. Honest feedback. The kind that makes you sweat and then makes you better.

choices.title: Join and commit fully
choices.body: The first session wrecks you. The second rebuilds you. By month three your work has jumped a level.

choices.title: Attend once, then ghost because it's scary
choices.body: You go once. The feedback is sharp. You say you'll come back. You don't.

choices.title: Join and eventually lead sessions
choices.body: You commit and within six months you're running critiques. The group becomes your design team.

title: The AI Knows Color Theory
body: An AI color palette generator suggests the exact combination you spent two days developing for the rebrand. Not similar. Exact. The same hex codes. The tool is free. Your salary is not. Your PM asks why the palette took two days.

choices.title: Go deeper into color science than AI can
choices.body: You study Munsell systems and chromatic adaptation. The depth becomes your moat.

choices.title: Use the generator, spend saved time on strategy
choices.body: You adopt the tool and redirect time to user research. The palette arrives in 30 seconds. The meaning still takes days.

choices.title: Accept that color selection is commoditized
choices.body: You stop defending palettes and start selling systems. The conversation shifts upstream.

title: The Portfolio Graveyard
body: You scroll your Behance. Most recent project: 18 months ago. Everything after that is under NDA. Your Behance is a museum of who you used to be when you still had time to post work.

choices.title: Update it with sanitized case studies
choices.body: You upload five anonymized projects. The algorithm rewards the burst. 200 views. It's something.

choices.title: Delete it, redirect to your personal site
choices.body: You nuke the profile. One less platform to maintain. One less ghost to feed.

choices.title: Leave it as-is, it's a time capsule now
choices.body: 2019-you had nice gradients though.

title: "Can You Also Do Motion?"
body: Your PM sees the competitor's animated product tour and asks about motion design. You have never opened After Effects. Lottie animations are a mystery. You say "I can look into it" because in-house designers say that and figure it out at midnight.

choices.title: Learn After Effects in a weekend, deliver
choices.body: You watch 14 hours of tutorials and deliver a simple micro-interaction. It moves. Moving is the whole requirement.

choices.title: Recommend hiring a motion specialist
choices.body: You make the case for a contractor. The budget gets approved for one month.

choices.title: Be honest about your skill gaps
choices.body: You say motion isn't your strength. The PM respects the honesty and finds another solution.

title: The All-Hands Imposter Moment
body: The CEO shows the product roadmap at all-hands. Your designs are on screen. The engineering team gets thanked by name. The design is described as "the team effort." The team is one person. You raise your hand from the back row.

choices.title: Speak up, claim credit professionally
choices.body: You say "happy to share the design process behind that" after the meeting. Two people notice. One is your skip-level.

choices.title: Stay quiet, the work speaks for itself
choices.body: The work speaks. Nobody hears it. Visibility requires volume, not just quality.

choices.title: Email the CEO directly with your contribution
choices.body: Bold. Risky. The CEO replies: "Great work." Two words. Enough.

title: The Pinterest Mood Board PRD
body: A PM sends a Pinterest board with 347 pins as the product brief. The pins include: minimalist Japanese architecture, a Lisa Frank folder, a brutalist building, and a golden retriever. "This is the vibe." It is four vibes. And a dog.

choices.title: Distill it to three coherent directions
choices.body: You sort their pins into themes. They say: "Can we combine all three?" And the dog.

choices.title: Pick the best pins, run with instinct
choices.body: You grab the 10 strongest references and build from there. The PM trusts you. This is rare.

choices.title: Ask them to narrow to 10 pins max
choices.body: They send 47. Progress.

title: The Marketing Team's Canva Files
body: Marketing sends a Canva link and asks you to "make it match the design system." It has 47 layers, all named Rectangle 1 through Rectangle 47. One color is #FF69B4. They used Hot Pink intentionally. This is your cross-functional partnership.

choices.title: Rebuild from scratch in Figma, log the hours
choices.body: You start over and bill it to the marketing sprint. Nobody argues.

choices.title: Work with what they gave you, adapt
choices.body: It takes twice as long. The hot pink stays. Marketing is happy.

choices.title: Create a brand template in Canva for them
choices.body: You build marketing-safe templates in their own tool. The niche is unglamorous and effective.

title: The 2026 Trend Report
body: A trends article lists: neobrutalism (again), AI-generated textures (obviously), and "human imperfection as aesthetic." Your PM sends it with "should we consider this?" You've been doing human imperfection since before it was a trend. You called it "being understaffed."

choices.title: Ride the trend, pitch it to leadership
choices.body: You present a trend-forward design direction. Leadership loves feeling current. The work is fine.

choices.title: Ignore trends, trust the design system
choices.body: Systems outlast trends. You keep building.

choices.title: Write an internal doc about timeless product design
choices.body: Timelessness is not a quarterly OKR. Moderate engagement from the three people who read internal docs.

title: The Equity Cliff
body: You just hit your one-year equity cliff. The stock is worth 40% of what it was when you signed. Your "total comp" is now mostly just your salary. The spreadsheet you made at offer time is a work of historical fiction.

choices.title: Ask for an equity refresh, present your case
choices.body: You make the argument. They refresh at 60% of original grant. Better than nothing. Barely.

choices.title: Start interviewing for a better package
choices.body: You take three recruiter calls. The market is rough but at least you have data.

choices.title: Accept it, equity was always a lottery ticket
choices.body: You stop checking the stock price. The salary is the salary. Everything else was fiction.

title: The Dark Pattern Request
body: Growth wants a cancellation flow that's intentionally confusing. "Make it hard to cancel, but legally." You are being asked to weaponize your design skills against your own users.

choices.title: Refuse, explain why dark patterns hurt retention
choices.body: You push back with data on trust erosion and churn. They compromise on "mildly inconvenient."

choices.title: Do it, collect the performance rating, feel nothing
choices.body: The flow is elegant in its cruelty. Cancellation rate drops 30%. You add it to the folder of things you'll never show.

choices.title: Escalate to your VP, blow the whistle
choices.body: You report it up the chain. Growth is annoyed. Your VP says "good catch." The pattern gets modified. Growth remembers.

title: The Open Source Design Project
body: An open-source project asks you to donate design work on weekends. The maintainer has 50k GitHub stars and zero design budget. The aesthetic is "developer chose the colors and also the layout and also the typography."

choices.title: Donate your time, redesign it properly
choices.body: 40 hours of weekend work. The community loves it. Your employer's IP policy may have opinions.

choices.title: Offer limited help, one evening a week
choices.body: You commit two hours weekly. Honest work at an honest pace. The project improves gradually.

choices.title: Decline, free work is a trap even for good causes
choices.body: The project continues to look like it was designed by a CI/CD pipeline.

title: "Just Clean These Up"
body: A client sends you 47 AI-generated mockups and asks you to "just clean them up a bit." The mockups have six-fingered icons, text that says "Lorem Ipsum Dolor Amet" in the hero, and a button that says "Click Here To Do The Thing." The client thinks they're 90% done. They are 90% confident.

choices.title: Clean them up, bill the hours
choices.body: You spend 30 hours fixing AI fever dreams. The client says "see, just needed a polish." Your invoice says otherwise.

choices.title: Explain why starting from scratch is faster
choices.body: You present a scope comparison. They say "but we already have designs?" The AI output is now the baseline. You're negotiating against a machine.

choices.title: Build an AI cleanup pipeline, sell it as a service
choices.body: You create a process for "AI design refinement" and charge a premium. Three more clients ask for it within a month. This is your job now.

title: Figma Generates Your Job
body: Figma ships an AI feature that generates entire design systems. Tokens, components, variants, documentation. It takes 30 seconds. Your design system took four months. The AI version is 80% as good. Your PM asks why the next one can't be done by Friday.

choices.title: Use it as a starting point, add the 20%
choices.body: You generate the base and spend two days on the craft layer. The result is better than either alone. Your timeline is now "two days" for what used to be a quarter.

choices.title: Refuse to use it, build by hand
choices.body: You build the system manually. It takes three weeks. It's measurably better. Leadership picks the AI version for the next project because it was faster.

choices.title: Become the person who configures it
choices.body: You learn every parameter and constraint. You're no longer the designer. You're the prompt engineer for a design tool. The title is new. The existential crisis is familiar.

title: "Why Can't AI Do This?"
body: In a sprint planning meeting, your PM asks: "Why can't we just use AI for the design?" The room goes quiet. Nobody pushes back. The engineering lead nods slowly. You explain the nuance of user research, interaction patterns, accessibility. The PM says "right, but for the simple screens?" All screens are simple to people who don't design them.

choices.title: Propose a hybrid workflow to stay relevant
choices.body: You present a plan where AI handles initial concepts and you handle refinement. The PM loves it. You've just negotiated yourself into half a job.

choices.title: Demonstrate what AI gets wrong with examples
choices.body: You run the PM's feature through three AI tools. The outputs are beautiful and wrong in ways that would cost $200k in engineering rework. The PM is convinced. For now.

choices.title: Say nothing, update your resume after the meeting
choices.body: The question wasn't really a question. It was an announcement wearing a question's clothes.

title: Your Portfolio Got Scraped
body: A friend sends you a link. An AI design tool is generating layouts in your style. Your exact style. The same spacing ratios, the same color philosophy, the same typographic hierarchy you spent a decade developing. It learned from your Dribbble, your Behance, your case studies. It does it faster. Some say better.

choices.title: Demand removal, pursue legal options
choices.body: You email the company. They reply: "Our model was trained on publicly available data." Your design language is now public domain. The law hasn't caught up.

choices.title: Evolve your style faster than AI can learn it
choices.body: You reinvent your visual language in a weekend sprint. The AI will learn this one too. You're in an arms race with your own ghost.

choices.title: Sell a course on the style before it's free
choices.body: You package your methodology into a paid workshop. $4k in the first month. You're monetizing your own obsolescence.

title: The Team Goes From Six to Two
body: Another round of "efficiency improvements." The design team was six, then three after last year's layoff. Now it's two: you and a junior who started three weeks ago. The Slack channel #design-team feels like a group chat between two people pretending a department exists.

choices.title: Absorb the workload, become the department
choices.body: You take on four people's worth of projects. The junior handles production. You handle everything else. The bus factor is one and you're driving.

choices.title: Make the case for AI tools to fill the gap
choices.body: You pitch AI-assisted design to replace the missing headcount. Leadership loves it. You've just automated your future colleagues out of existence.

choices.title: Start interviewing while you still have leverage
choices.body: A shrinking team is a signal, not a challenge. You take three calls. The market is worse than you expected.

title: One Thousand Variations
body: Your PM demos a tool that generates 1,000 design variations for a landing page in 40 seconds. You spent three days on four directions. Your directions are better. The PM knows this. The PM also knows that 1,000 variations cost $0.12 and your three days cost $3,000.

choices.title: Position yourself as the curator, not creator
choices.body: You offer to evaluate and refine the AI output. The work is faster. The craft is thinner. Your title doesn't change but your job description rewrites itself.

choices.title: Prove quality matters with A/B test data
choices.body: You A/B test your version against the best AI variation. Yours converts 23% better. Leadership says "interesting" and ships the AI version because it was ready two days earlier.

choices.title: Learn to generate better variations than the tool
choices.body: You master the prompt engineering. Your AI-assisted output beats both. You've become a centaur. Half human, half machine. Fully confused.

title: AI Handles Design, You Handle QA
body: Your manager redefines your role in a 1:1. "We're moving to AI-first design. We need you for quality assurance." You are now the person who checks if the AI's work is good enough. Your title is still "Senior Product Designer" but your job is proofreading a machine.

choices.title: Accept the pivot, become the quality layer
choices.body: You build a rubric for evaluating AI design output. It's thorough, professional, and feels like writing your own obituary.

choices.title: Negotiate to keep creative ownership of key features
choices.body: You carve out the flagship product as human-designed. Everything else is AI. Your territory shrinks sprint by sprint.

choices.title: Refuse the new role, start job hunting
choices.body: You say you're a designer, not a reviewer. Your manager says "the market is evolving." So is your LinkedIn status.

title: The Free AI Design Tool
body: A startup launches a free AI design tool. Upload a screenshot of any app, it generates a complete redesign in your brand colors with proper components. Product Hunt #1. Your PM sends it to you with a smiley face. Your entire workflow just became a feature in someone else's product.

choices.title: Learn it deeply, become the internal expert
choices.body: You spend a weekend mastering every parameter. Monday you present a workflow that cuts design time by 60%. Your value is now teaching others to not need you.

choices.title: Write a detailed comparison showing its limitations
choices.body: You document every failure mode. Accessibility violations, inconsistent spacing, nonsensical user flows. The doc is thorough. Nobody reads past page one.

choices.title: Use it and don't tell anyone
choices.body: You adopt it quietly and spend the freed hours on strategic work nobody asked for. Your output increases. Your secret stays.

title: Your Followers Are Studying You
body: Your Dribbble analytics spike: 400 new followers in a week. You investigate. They're mostly AI accounts with names like "DesignFlow_v3" and "UIHarvest." They're not following you for inspiration. They're scraping your work to train models. Your audience is a dataset.

choices.title: Make your portfolio private, protect the work
choices.body: You lock everything down. Your visibility drops. A recruiter says she can't see your work. The trade-off is real.

choices.title: Watermark everything, poison the training data
choices.body: You add invisible watermarks and deliberate artifacts. It's guerrilla warfare against machines learning your taste.

choices.title: Post more, lean into the attention
choices.body: If they're going to learn from you, make the curriculum worth studying. Your engagement metrics look great on paper.

title: The AI Design Review
body: Engineering adds an AI step to the design review pipeline. It evaluates your mockups for accessibility, consistency, and "design quality" on a 1-100 scale. Your latest work scored 73. The AI-generated alternative scored 81. Your PM shares both scores in Slack without comment.

choices.title: Challenge the scoring criteria publicly
choices.body: You question the rubric. The scoring weighs pixel consistency over user empathy. The AI wins on metrics. Users aren't metrics. Yet.

choices.title: Optimize your work for the AI reviewer
choices.body: You adjust your process to score higher. Your designs become measurably better and immeasurably less interesting.

choices.title: Propose a user-testing component to the score
choices.body: You add real user feedback to the rubric. Humans still prefer human work. For now.

title: The AI Brand Book
body: Marketing creates an entire brand book using Midjourney and GPT. Photography, illustrations, voice guidelines, color rationale. It took two days. It's coherent and soulless in a way that's hard to articulate and impossible to prove. The CMO presents it at all-hands as "our new creative direction."

choices.title: Point out what's missing, fight for craft
choices.body: You present a side-by-side with hand-crafted alternatives. The difference is real. The budget for hand-crafted is not.

choices.title: Adapt it, make it actually work
choices.body: You take the AI brand book and fix the 200 things nobody noticed were wrong. The CMO thanks you for "polishing it."

choices.title: Let it ship, document what happens
choices.body: The brand inconsistencies compound over three months. You keep a log. The redesign request arrives on schedule.

title: Clients Stop Requesting Mockups
body: Three freelance clients cancel mockup projects in the same week. All give the same reason: "We're using AI for initial designs now." One adds: "But we might need you for the tricky stuff later." The tricky stuff is a smaller market than the easy stuff. The easy stuff was your rent.

choices.title: Pivot to strategy and research consulting
choices.body: You rebrand as a "product design strategist." The hourly rate goes up. The volume goes down. The math is uncertain.

choices.title: Offer AI-assisted design at lower rates
choices.body: You cut your rate 40% and use AI for the commodity work. More clients, less margin, less craft. The treadmill speeds up.

choices.title: Double down on the full-service day job
choices.body: Freelance was insurance. The insurance just expired. Your employer's Slack has never felt more like a lifeline.

title: The Junior Gets AI'd
body: The junior designer who started three weeks ago just got laid off. The reason given: "We're using AI tools to handle production design." She cries in the parking lot. You helped hire her. The team is now one: you. Again.

choices.title: Advocate loudly for her, burn political capital
choices.body: You escalate to your VP. They say the decision is final. Your reputation as "difficult" grows. Your conscience is clear.

choices.title: Help her find another role quietly
choices.body: You make twelve introductions over the weekend. She gets two interviews. The industry is smaller than the org chart suggests.

choices.title: Say nothing, protect your own position
choices.body: Survival math. The guilt arrives on a delay, like emotional latency.

title: The Auto-Generated Design System
body: A product manager shows you a demo: an AI tool that scans your production code and generates a complete design system from what's already shipped. Tokens, components, documentation. It reverse-engineers your work and packages it without you. The PM says "this could save us a quarter."

choices.title: Audit the output, prove it needs human oversight
choices.body: You find 47 inconsistencies. The PM says "that's what the next version will fix." You realize you're QA-ing your own replacement.

choices.title: Adopt it and position yourself as the curator
choices.body: You become the taste layer. AI generates, you approve. The creative act is now a yes/no decision. A thousand times a sprint.

choices.title: Propose a human-AI collaborative system instead
choices.body: You design a workflow where AI handles structure and you handle intent. It works. For now, the collaboration feels real.

title: Performance Review: AI Edition
body: Performance review season. The new evaluation framework includes "AI tool adoption rate" as a metric. Designers are scored on how efficiently they use AI in their workflow. Refusing AI tools is now a performance issue. Your craft is a liability on a spreadsheet.

choices.title: Game the metric, use AI for everything possible
choices.body: Your adoption rate hits 94%. Your designs look like everything else. The review is excellent. The work is forgettable.

choices.title: Push back on the metric in the review
choices.body: You argue that output quality should matter more than tool adoption. Your manager agrees privately and scores you on the metric anyway.

choices.title: Document your AI-free wins as case studies
choices.body: You build a portfolio of projects where human craft outperformed AI alternatives. The evidence is compelling. The policy doesn't change.

title: The Job Posting That Isn't
body: A recruiter sends you a job listing for "AI Design Operations Lead." The role: manage AI tools that generate designs, review output, maintain brand consistency. Zero Figma. Zero pixels. Zero creation. The salary is 20% more than your current role. The future of design management is managing machines.

choices.title: Interview, see what it's really like
choices.body: The hiring manager shows you the dashboard. Thousands of designs generated per day. Your job: thumb up or thumb down. Tinder for UI. The salary is real.

choices.title: Decline, you're a maker not a manager of machines
choices.body: You reply: "I appreciate it but I still want to design." The recruiter says "that's getting rarer." They mean the job. And the desire.

choices.title: Forward it to a designer friend who needs work
choices.body: They take the role. Two months later they say it's "fine." Fine is the ceiling now.

title: The Conference Is All AI Now
body: You attend a design conference. Every talk is about AI. "AI-First Design Systems." "Prompting as Design Practice." "Post-Craft Design Leadership." The word "craft" appears only in historical context. Like "blacksmithing" or "calligraphy." A speaker says "the last generation of hand-designers" and means you.

choices.title: Network with others who feel the same way
choices.body: You find a group at the hotel bar. All senior designers. All rattled. The solidarity is warm and the implications are cold.

choices.title: Give a lightning talk defending human craft
choices.body: You sign up for an open slot. Five minutes on why taste can't be automated. The applause is loud. The conference hashtag moves on in 20 minutes.

choices.title: Leave early, the future doesn't need your attendance
choices.body: You grab the tote bag and walk out during the "AI Design Ethics" panel. The panel has no designers on it.

title: The AI Design Agency
body: A new agency launches: "Full product design in 48 hours, AI-powered, $2,000 flat rate." Your project timelines are 6-8 weeks at $40k+. They show a case study. The work is competent. Not great, not terrible. Exactly good enough. Your clients start asking why your timeline is so long.

choices.title: Compete on quality, raise your rates
choices.body: You position yourself as premium. Three clients leave for the AI agency. Two new ones come specifically because you're human. The math is tighter.

choices.title: Offer a "fast track" AI-assisted tier
choices.body: You add a cheaper, faster option using AI tools. The premium tier gets lonelier. The fast track keeps the lights on.

choices.title: Study their process, learn what they're actually doing
choices.body: You reverse-engineer their workflow. It's AI generation plus a human designer doing exactly what you'd do, at 1/10th your rate, in a different timezone.

title: The Voice of the Brand Is AI
body: Your PM announces that all in-app microcopy will be AI-generated going forward. Your carefully crafted button labels, error messages, and onboarding text will be replaced by a model that generates "on-brand" copy in milliseconds. You point out that your error messages had personality. The PM says "personality is a prompt parameter now."

choices.title: Write the prompt guidelines for the AI
choices.body: You create a voice document so detailed it's essentially a creative writing course for a machine. The AI follows it well enough that you can't tell the difference. You wish you could.

choices.title: Argue for human-written copy on key screens
choices.body: You negotiate that onboarding, error states, and empty states stay human-written. Everything else is AI. Your domain shrinks by the sprint.

choices.title: Accept it, focus only on visual design
choices.body: Words were never your job anyway. Except they were. Except now they're not. The boundary between disciplines was the first thing AI dissolved.

title: User Research Gets Automated
body: The UX researcher gets replaced by an AI that conducts user interviews via chat, synthesizes findings, and generates personas. The output is thorough and unsettling. The personas have names, backstories, pain points. None of them are real people. Your PM says the insights are "good enough." Design without real users is architecture without gravity.

choices.title: Conduct your own guerrilla research to supplement
choices.body: You interview five real users on your lunch break. Their feedback contradicts the AI personas. Nobody wants to hear that.

choices.title: Use the AI research but validate the key assumptions
choices.body: You cherry-pick the AI insights and verify the critical ones. Hybrid research. The PM is satisfied. Your inner researcher is not.

choices.title: Accept the new normal, design for fictional people
choices.body: The personas are fictional. The product ships to real humans. The gap between research and reality is someone else's problem now.

title: AI Skips Accessibility
body: The AI design tool generates beautiful interfaces that fail every accessibility audit. Contrast ratios, focus states, screen reader support -- all missing. Your PM says "we'll fix it later." Later is when the lawsuit arrives. You are the only person in the room who knows what WCAG stands for.

choices.title: Build an accessibility review into the AI pipeline
choices.body: You create an automated a11y check that runs after every AI generation. It catches 70% of issues. The other 30% still needs you. For now.

choices.title: Sound the alarm to legal and leadership
choices.body: You write a risk assessment. Legal thanks you. Engineering adds a11y to their backlog. It sits at priority 4 for two quarters.

choices.title: Let it ship, document that you warned them
choices.body: You send a CYA email and watch it go live. The complaint form gets its first submission within a week.

title: Handoff to the Machine
body: Your engineering team implements a system where AI converts your Figma designs directly into production code. No developer interpretation needed. The code is clean. The implementation is pixel-perfect. You should be thrilled. Instead you feel like a sketch that got traced. The artisan-to-factory pipeline is complete.

choices.title: Focus on the parts machines can't translate
choices.body: Motion, delight, micro-interactions that require human judgment. Your domain narrows to the poetic. It might be enough.

choices.title: Learn the AI-to-code pipeline, own both sides
choices.body: You become the only person who understands design AND the translation layer. Indispensable through comprehensiveness.

choices.title: Celebrate the win, your designs ship perfectly now
choices.body: No more "the engineer interpreted it wrong." The implementation matches. The irony is that perfection makes you feel less needed.

title: Keeping Up With Machine Speed
body: AI generates concepts at inhuman speed. Your sprint velocity is now benchmarked against a tool that doesn't sleep, eat, or have existential crises. You're doing twice the work you did last year. Your PM says "we should be able to do more now." More is the only direction.

choices.title: Set boundaries, explain human design has a clock speed
choices.body: You tell your manager that quality requires time. They schedule a meeting to discuss "efficiency opportunities." The meeting is 30 minutes you could have spent designing.

choices.title: Match the pace using AI, sacrifice depth
choices.body: You hit the velocity targets. Every design looks like every other design. The product becomes a screensaver with a business model.

choices.title: Find a role that values slow, careful work
choices.body: Healthcare, government, fintech. Industries where moving fast breaks things that matter. The pay is less. The pressure is different.

title: Your Side Project Gets AI'd
body: Your Figma template store was making $800/month. An AI tool just launched that generates custom Figma templates for free. Your sales dropped 70% in two weeks. The passive income dream lasted eight months. The AI version of your templates looks like your templates because it literally learned from your templates.

choices.title: Pivot to workshops teaching the human layer
choices.body: You sell what AI can't replicate: judgment, context, the ability to explain why. The first cohort sells out. The second doesn't.

choices.title: Shut it down and grieve
choices.body: You archive the Gumroad page. Eight months of late nights, gone in two weeks. The efficiency of creative destruction is not comforting when you're the thing being destroyed.

choices.title: Add AI-proof features, try to stay ahead
choices.body: You add hand-crafted micro-interactions and video walkthroughs. Sales stabilize at 30% of peak. The hamster wheel has no exit.

title: Thirty Seconds to a Design System
body: Your VP pulls up an AI tool in a meeting and generates a complete design system live. Tokens, components, spacing scale, color palette, dark mode. Thirty seconds. The room applauds. Your four-month design system sits in Figma with 2,400 hours logged. The VP says "we should use this for the next one."

choices.title: Propose merging the best of both
choices.body: You combine your system's strategic decisions with the AI's execution speed. The result is better than either alone. The PM credits the AI tool in the all-hands.

choices.title: Show the 47 things the AI system got wrong
choices.body: You audit the AI system line by line. 47 accessibility violations, 12 inconsistencies, 3 outright errors. The VP says "we'll iterate." Iterate is free when the tool is free.

choices.title: Accept it, redirect your energy upstream
choices.body: If systems can be generated, the value is in knowing which system to generate. Strategy over pixels. The shift feels like retreat.

title: The AI That Designs Better Than You
body: A new AI tool generates app designs that are, objectively, more consistent than your work. Not more creative. Not more meaningful. But more consistent. Pixel-perfect spacing, flawless alignment, zero drift between components. The things you spent years training yourself to do. The AI does them without trying because trying is a human concept.

choices.title: Focus on the things that require trying
choices.body: Empathy, context, rebellion against convention, the choice to break a grid because the moment calls for it. The domain of intention.

choices.title: Use the tool to handle consistency, you handle meaning
choices.body: The partnership works. AI does the math. You do the feeling. The output is the best work of your career.

choices.title: Compete head-to-head, prove humans still win
choices.body: You challenge the AI to a design-off. Yours is better. You post the comparison. 4,000 likes. The AI doesn't know it lost. It doesn't know anything.

title: The Intern Who Prompts
body: The summer intern doesn't use Figma. She prompts. She generates 50 screen concepts before lunch. She's never opened the design system documentation. She doesn't know what a token is. Her output is prolific and rootless. Your PM says she's "incredibly productive." Productive is the only metric that survived the transition.

choices.title: Teach her the fundamentals she's missing
choices.body: You pair with her for a week. She learns grids, hierarchy, accessibility. Her AI output gets 10x better. You just made AI design actually work. The feeling is complicated.

choices.title: Adopt her workflow, catch up to the new speed
choices.body: You learn to prompt alongside Figma. Your output doubles. Your relationship with your own craft changes permanently.

choices.title: Let her process stand, protect your own
choices.body: Two workflows coexist. Hers is faster. Yours is deeper. The PM values both until budget forces a choice.

title: The AI Gives You Design Feedback
body: Your company integrates an AI design critic into the review process. It evaluates your mockups and provides suggestions: "Consider increasing contrast ratio on CTA buttons." "The visual hierarchy suggests secondary actions are primary." The feedback is correct. Getting notes from a machine about your craft is like getting a cooking lesson from a microwave.

choices.title: Integrate the feedback, swallow the pride
choices.body: The AI catches things you missed. Your work improves. The process feels like being edited by autocorrect -- helpful and humbling in equal measure.

choices.title: Argue that design critique requires human context
choices.body: You present cases where the AI's suggestions would worsen the design. Context-dependent decisions that require understanding WHY the user is there, not just WHAT they see.

choices.title: Use it but never mention it to other designers
choices.body: Like spellcheck, you adopt it silently. The stigma of needing AI feedback is real in design circles. The utility is also real.

title: Everyone Is Freelance Now
body: Three designer friends got laid off in the same month. All went freelance. Not by choice -- by elimination. The freelance market is flooded with senior designers competing for projects that AI hasn't eaten yet. Rates drop 30%. "The gig economy" used to be a choice. Now it's a diagnosis.

choices.title: Help organize a freelance collective
choices.body: You pool resources with five designers. Shared leads, shared clients, shared dread. Together you're an agency. Apart you're five people refreshing Upwork.

choices.title: Stay employed, count your blessings
choices.body: Your W-2 is a privilege now. Health insurance, 401k match, predictable deposits. The golden handcuffs are comfortable when everyone else is barefoot.

choices.title: Prepare your own freelance safety net
choices.body: You start moonlighting on weekends. Three clients. Small projects. If the layoff comes, you'll have a running start.

title: The Newsletter Pays Off
body: Your design newsletter just hit 500 subscribers. A VP of Product at another company emails: "I've been reading your stuff for months. We need a design lead." Side projects with inboxes become escape hatches.

choices.title: Interview, leverage it for a raise
choices.body: You get an offer and use it to negotiate a 25% raise at your current company. Capitalism is a negotiation.

choices.title: Explore sponsored newsletter partnerships
choices.body: A design tool pays $3k/month for six months to sponsor your newsletter. The side income becomes real.

choices.title: Refer the role to a friend, keep the newsletter pure
choices.body: You send the job lead to a designer friend. They get hired. Your network strengthens.

title: Side Project Gets Traction
body: Your Figma plugin just crossed $1k/month in revenue. You spend zero hours on it now. You stare at the Stripe dashboard like it's a nature documentary. Your employment agreement might have something to say about this.

choices.title: Double down, build a product suite
choices.body: Revenue hits $3k/month. You start calling yourself a product designer/founder. Your employer doesn't know.

choices.title: Keep it passive, focus on the day job
choices.body: You let the plugin run on autopilot. Balance feels possible.

choices.title: Open-source it, build goodwill
choices.body: Downloads triple. Three people reach out to hire you because of it.

title: The Collective Gets a Client
body: Your design collective gets approached for a consulting project. Real stakes. Real budget. The group chat goes quiet, then very loud. Your employer's moonlighting policy enters the conversation.

choices.title: Lead the project, take creative direction
choices.body: The pressure is immense. The work is the best you've ever done. Your day job suffers slightly.

choices.title: Play support, let someone else lead
choices.body: Less glory, less stress, same after-hours commitment.

choices.title: Decline, the risk is too high with your employer
choices.body: The project goes to someone else. You wonder what if.

title: Going Viral Is a Job Now
body: Your post about being the last designer went viral. 12k likes. 400 replies. Eight podcast invitations. Three death threats. You posted an opinion and now you have a constituency. Your employer's comms team has questions.

choices.title: Ride the wave, book the podcasts
choices.body: You do four appearances. Your audience doubles. Your day job suffers. HR sends a friendly reminder about social media policy.

choices.title: Go silent, let it die naturally
choices.body: You mute everything and work. The discourse moves on. Your PM is relieved.

choices.title: Write a follow-up that's more nuanced
choices.body: It gets 1/10th the engagement. The truth is boring. You feel good about it.

title: The Network Compounds
body: The developer you met at the coffee shop referred you to a hiring manager. The hiring manager connected you to their VP. Your network is compounding while your company is contracting.

choices.title: Take every meeting, explore everything
choices.body: Three become real conversations. Your calendar is full. Your manager notices your distraction.

choices.title: Be selective, only take the best fit
choices.body: You decline two and pursue the one that excites you. Quality over quantity.

choices.title: Ask for introductions instead of opportunities
choices.body: Your network grows. The opportunities come later, bigger.

title: The Credit Card Reckoning
body: You put last month's bootcamp course, conference ticket, and three design tool subscriptions on a credit card you forgot you were paying interest on. Your professional development has a payment plan.

choices.title: Get the company to reimburse, push hard
choices.body: You submit everything to L&D. They cover 70%. The remaining 30% stings less.

choices.title: Take on overtime work to cover the balance
choices.body: You volunteer for an extra project. The credit card gets paid. Your weekends don't.

choices.title: Ask a friend for a short-term loan
choices.body: You pay it back in three weeks. The friendship gets more honest.

title: "UX Designer" Removed From Job Boards
body: You search for "UX Designer" on three job boards. 12 results. Last year: 340. The title is being replaced by "AI Design Operations," "Prompt Design Lead," and "Human Experience Curator." Your ten years of UX experience now qualifies you for a role that didn't exist six months ago and pays 40% less.

choices.title: Rebrand yourself, adapt the language
choices.body: You update your LinkedIn to "Product Experience Strategist." The same recruiter who ignored you last month reaches out. Titles are spells and you just learned a new one.

choices.title: Hold the line, call yourself a designer
choices.body: You keep "Product Designer" and watch the callbacks dry up. Integrity is expensive when rent is due.

choices.title: Start applying for adjacent roles
choices.body: Product management, design engineering, creative direction. The skills transfer. The identity doesn't.

title: "Taste Consultant" Is Your New Title
body: A company offers you a role: "Taste Consultant." Your job is to choose which AI-generated design to ship. Eight hours a day selecting from infinite options. The pay is 60% of your old salary. The job description says "discerning eye required." Your decade of craft reduced to a thumb and a preference.

choices.title: Take it, money is money
choices.body: You start Monday. By Wednesday you've approved 400 designs. Your eye is still sharp. Your soul is somewhere in the reject pile.

choices.title: Negotiate for creative input, not just curation
choices.body: You propose a hybrid role: curate AI output AND design the critical screens. They give you 20% creative. It's better than zero.

choices.title: Decline, find a company that still employs designers
choices.body: The list is getting shorter every month. You find one. They're in healthcare. The UI is ugly in ways that keep humans alive.

title: The Industrial Design Pivot
body: A friend who used to design apps now designs furniture. Physical objects. Things AI can't generate into existence. She makes $60k less but her work exists in three dimensions. "The screen is AI territory," she says over coffee. "I went where the robots can't follow." You look at your hands. They used to draw.

choices.title: Take a ceramics class, test the waters
choices.body: Saturday mornings, clay under your fingernails. The objects you make are terrible and yours. Nobody can generate them in 30 seconds.

choices.title: Explore industrial design programs online
choices.body: You enroll in an evening program. The skills are adjacent. The learning curve is real. The physical world has a different grammar.

choices.title: Stay digital, the screen is where the money is
choices.body: Your friend is happy. Your friend also doesn't have a 401k anymore. You stay in the burning building because it's air-conditioned.

title: The AI Trained On Your Work
body: The company's internal AI design tool was trained on every Figma file in the company's history. Your files. Your systems. Your decisions. It now generates designs that look like you designed them. Because you did. Three years ago. The model is you, minus the salary and the health insurance.

choices.title: Demand compensation for the training data
choices.body: Legal says your work belongs to the company. Your design taste, your visual instincts, your years of refinement -- all "work product." You signed the IP clause in 2023.

choices.title: Collaborate with your digital ghost
choices.body: You start using the model as a starting point. It's like pair-designing with a past version of yourself. Productive and haunting.

choices.title: Deliberately design differently from the model
choices.body: You break every pattern the AI learned from you. New grids, new ratios, new everything. Your work becomes unrecognizable. Also unpredictable. Also better.

title: "Pivot to Industrial" Is "Learn to Code"
body: LinkedIn is full of ex-UX designers posting about their new careers in architecture, furniture, interior design, and landscape architecture. The comments say "so brave" and "the future is physical." Pivoting to industrial design is the new "learn to code" -- advice that sounds empowering and costs three years of your life.

choices.title: Start a physical design practice on the side
choices.body: You take on a signage project for a local restaurant. $800. The work is tangible. The pay is symbolic. The satisfaction is real.

choices.title: Stay digital, refuse the narrative
choices.body: You're not going to abandon a decade of expertise because LinkedIn told you to. The pivot narrative is for people writing about work, not doing it.

choices.title: Explore hybrid physical-digital design
choices.body: You find a niche: designing physical spaces that integrate with digital products. Wayfinding systems, interactive installations. The intersection is small and uncontested.

title: A Product Ships Without a Designer
body: A competitor launches a fully designed product. The UI is clean, consistent, accessible. Their team page lists no designers. The About page says "designed by our AI-native workflow." The reviews say "beautiful and intuitive." You check the source code. It was generated end-to-end.

choices.title: Study it obsessively, find what's missing
choices.body: You find the gaps: no delight, no surprise, no personality. It's competent in the way a form letter is competent. But competent ships and personality doesn't.

choices.title: Write about it, sound the alarm
choices.body: Your essay goes semi-viral. The responses split between "this is the future" and "this is the end." Both are right.

choices.title: Call your designer friends, process it together
choices.body: You get four people on a video call. Everyone is shaken. Nobody has a solution. The company is real.

title: The Great Salary Compression
body: Design salaries have dropped 35% across the industry in 18 months. Supply and demand: when AI can do 70% of the work, the remaining 30% isn't worth what it used to be. Your recruiter says "the market has corrected." Corrected means you're worth less. Mathematically. Not morally.

choices.title: Accept the new rates, you need income
choices.body: You take a contract at the new normal. The work is the same. The compensation reflects a world that values your skills less. You design for people who can't tell what's missing.

choices.title: Specialize in what commands premium rates
choices.body: Accessibility, complex systems, regulated industries. The niches where AI can't operate unsupervised. The work is harder. The rates hold.

choices.title: Leave the industry entirely, retrain
choices.body: You look at nursing programs, trade schools, anything with a floor under the wages. The brochures feel like science fiction.

title: AI Users Test Your Designs
body: Your company replaces real user testing with AI-simulated users. Thousands of synthetic personas "test" your designs and provide feedback. The data is statistically significant and emotionally empty. A simulated user says your onboarding "feels cold." An AI told you your design lacks feeling. You laugh. Then you don't.

choices.title: Insist on real user testing for key flows
choices.body: You fight for a budget to test with actual humans. Three sessions, $900. The insights are worth more than 10,000 synthetic responses. Your PM is not sure about that.

choices.title: Design for the AI testers, optimize for metrics
choices.body: You learn to make designs that score well with the synthetic users. The real users are different. But nobody's asking them anymore.

choices.title: Add a human empathy layer to the testing pipeline
choices.body: You create a framework that combines AI data with real human interviews. It's better. It's also more expensive and slower. The market picks fast and cheap.

title: The Design Bootcamps Close
body: Three major UX bootcamps announce closure in the same week. The pipeline of new designers has shut off. The junior roles they trained people for don't exist anymore. A bootcamp founder posts: "We taught people to be better than they needed to be for jobs that no longer exist." The eulogy for an industry.

choices.title: Offer your own mentorship program
choices.body: You create a small cohort. Eight people. Real projects. The curriculum is "surviving as a designer in 2027." It's honest and painful.

choices.title: Feel grateful you got in before the door closed
choices.body: Survivor's guilt is real. The juniors you mentored are being told their career was a mirage.

choices.title: Write about the industry's failure to adapt
choices.body: Your essay connects bootcamp closures to the broader collapse of the knowledge worker pipeline. A publication picks it up.

title: The Collective Goes Physical
body: Your design collective pivots from digital to physical projects. Exhibition design, pop-up spaces, environmental graphics. The work is harder, the pay is less, and AI can't do it. The first project is designing a community garden. You stand in dirt sketching on paper. Something old wakes up.

choices.title: Go all in on physical design projects
choices.body: You take on signage, wayfinding, and spatial design. The margins are thin. The work is real in a way screens stopped being.

choices.title: Keep one foot in digital, hedge your bets
choices.body: Weekdays: AI-assisted product design. Weekends: letterpress and spatial work. Two identities. One is dying. One is being born.

choices.title: Document the transition for other designers
choices.body: You photograph every physical project and write about the pivot. The content resonates with thousands of designers feeling the same pull.

title: The Designerless Startup Wins
body: A startup with zero designers and an AI design pipeline just closed a $40M Series B. Their product looks good. Not great. Good. The investors say "design is solved" in the press release. Your field is now a solved problem. Like spell-checking.

choices.title: Rage-design something that proves them wrong
choices.body: You spend a weekend on a personal project so beautiful it hurts. You post it. 2,000 likes. The startup is worth $40M. The likes are worth nothing. The work is worth everything.

choices.title: Study what they're actually missing
choices.body: You do a UX audit of their product. 43 usability issues. The investors don't care. The users do. Someone will pay to fix those issues. Eventually.

choices.title: Consider the possibility they might be right
choices.body: Not that design is solved. But that "good enough" design is. And that you've been overvaluing craft in a market that values speed.

title: "Artisanal UX" Is a Thing Now
body: A luxury brand hires you for "artisanal UX design." Human-designed, human-coded, certified AI-free. Their customers pay $400 for a candle. They'll pay extra for an app that was made by a person. Your craft just became a luxury good. The irony is so thick you could charge for it.

choices.title: Take the gig, embrace the luxury positioning
choices.body: The work is exquisite and the client is insufferable. They want every pixel "hand-placed" and documented. The rate is triple your normal. You design like it's 2019.

choices.title: Use it as a case study for human-designed premium
choices.body: You document the entire process. The case study becomes a manifesto for craft. Other luxury brands reach out.

choices.title: Decline, you don't want to be a boutique
choices.body: Design for the rich while everyone else gets AI slop. The class dynamics of your profession are now literal.

title: The Empathy Consultant
body: A job listing: "Human Empathy Consultant." Requirements: design background, ability to articulate human needs to AI systems. You'd be the interface between what people feel and what machines generate. The job is explaining emotions to software. The salary is half what designers used to make.

choices.title: Apply, this is where the puck is going
choices.body: You get the job. Day one: you explain to an AI system why a loading spinner causes anxiety. The AI adjusts. You feel like a therapist for software.

choices.title: Freelance the empathy work, keep your independence
choices.body: You offer "human insight audits" to AI-first companies. Three clients in the first month. The market for feelings is smaller than the market for pixels.

choices.title: Refuse, you're a designer not a translator
choices.body: The distinction between designer and "person who explains design to machines" is real to you and invisible to the market.

title: The AI Client
body: A company contacts you with an unusual brief: design an interface for an AI agent to use. The end user isn't human. It's another AI. The design requirements include "machine-readable affordances" and "sub-100ms visual parsing." You're designing for an audience that doesn't have eyes.

choices.title: Take the project, the money's real even if the user isn't
choices.body: You design interfaces optimized for machine perception. The aesthetic is alien. Beautiful in a way humans don't need. The check clears.

choices.title: Propose a human-AI hybrid interface instead
choices.body: You argue that someone will eventually need to audit the AI-to-AI interaction. They agree. The dashboard has one human user: the person making sure the machines play nice.

choices.title: Decline, you design for humans
choices.body: You say no. They find someone else. You wonder if the next generation of designers will think this is normal.

title: The Designers' Union
body: A national coalition of designers is organizing. They want minimum rates, AI disclosure requirements, and training data compensation. The founding document reads like a Geneva Convention for creative workers. Your employer's PR team sends a memo about "staying neutral." Neutral is a side.

choices.title: Join publicly, risk your position
choices.body: You sign the open letter. 4,000 designers join. Your company's HR sends a friendly follow-up about "company values." The line between activism and career suicide is one LinkedIn post.

choices.title: Support anonymously, protect your income
choices.body: You donate and share resources under a pseudonym. Courage takes many forms. Some of them are anonymous.

choices.title: Stay out of it, focus on survival
choices.body: You watch from the sidelines. The union wins small concessions. You benefit without risking anything. The guilt is manageable.

title: The Taste Question
body: You spent ten years developing taste. Color intuition. Spacing feel. Typography instinct. AI has taste now. Or something indistinguishable from it. A model trained on every design in history has preferences. They're not random. They're not yours. Was your taste just pattern matching all along?

choices.title: Go deeper into what makes your taste yours
choices.body: You study your own decisions. The patterns are real. But so is something else: the willingness to break them. AI optimizes. You occasionally choose to be wrong on purpose. That's the gap.

choices.title: Accept that taste is pattern matching, move on
choices.body: The existential crisis resolves into pragmatism. You're still fast. You still ship. The philosophical questions can wait for a sabbatical you can't afford.

choices.title: Talk to other creatives about it, you need the words
choices.body: A painter friend says: "Cameras didn't kill painting. They freed it." You're not sure the analogy holds. But you needed to hear it.

title: Hand-Drawn Wireframes Are Luxury
body: A client asks you to present hand-drawn wireframes. On paper. They want the "human process" documented and photographed for their brand story. Your sketches cost more than the AI-generated final product. The rough draft is now more valuable than the finished work. The world has inverted.

choices.title: Charge premium for the hand-drawn process
choices.body: You triple your rate for hand-drawn discovery. Three clients a quarter. The scarcity of human craft is your moat.

choices.title: Offer it as a workshop experience
choices.body: Teams pay $5k to watch you sketch and think aloud. They're not buying wireframes. They're buying proximity to a process that's disappearing.

choices.title: Keep it private, drawing is for you now
choices.body: The sketchbook is the last space where nobody is watching. Not the PM, not the AI, not the algorithm. Ink on paper. Yours.

title: The Last Design Job Posting
body: Your company posts an opening for a designer. It gets 2,400 applications in 48 hours. A third of applicants are senior designers from FAANG. The role pays less than an entry-level engineer. The hiring manager says "we're spoiled for choice." The choice is between people who used to have careers.

choices.title: Offer to help screen applicants
choices.body: You review 200 portfolios. Eighty are better than yours was when you started. The talent pool is an ocean. The shore is eroding.

choices.title: Advocate for better comp for the role
choices.body: You make the case to HR that underpaying designers means getting someone desperate, not someone good. They raise it 10%. Still not enough.

choices.title: Use it as leverage for your own raise
choices.body: 2,400 people want your chair. That's not leverage, that's a reminder of how replaceable you are. But you frame it as institutional knowledge. It works. Barely.

title: The AI Joins Your Critique Group
body: Someone in your critique group starts submitting AI-generated work for feedback. The group debates whether to allow it. The work is good. Not distinguishable from human work. The purpose of the group -- honest human feedback on human craft -- feels suddenly quaint. Like a book club for scrolls.

choices.title: Propose a human-only rule for the group
choices.body: The vote passes 4-2. Two members leave. The remaining four produce their most personal work in months. Constraints breed honesty.

choices.title: Accept AI work but require disclosure
choices.body: The hybrid format works for a while. Then everyone starts using AI and disclosing it. The critique becomes a prompt review session.

choices.title: Leave the group, find something more grounded
choices.body: You join a figure drawing class instead. Charcoal on paper. No plugins. No undo.

title: Every UI Has Been Designed
body: A design research paper claims that AI models have now generated every possible standard UI pattern combination. Dashboard layouts, settings pages, onboarding flows -- the space of conventional design has been exhausted. Originality in UI is now either impossible or requires breaking conventions that exist for good reason.

choices.title: Design unconventionally, break the patterns
choices.body: You create interfaces that violate every standard. Some are brilliant. Most are confusing. The line between innovation and bad UX has never been thinner.

choices.title: Accept that UI is a solved space, focus on UX
choices.body: The pixels are commoditized. The understanding of why people do things is not. You shift upstream permanently.

choices.title: Find beauty in curation, not creation
choices.body: If every possible UI exists, design becomes choosing well. The designer as curator. The museum of infinite rooms.

title: The Project Gets AI'd Mid-Sprint
body: You're three weeks into the most meaningful project of the year. The VP walks in: "We're going AI-first on this one, the timeline moved up." Your three weeks of research, sketches, and prototypes get replaced by a 45-minute AI generation session. The output is 70% of what yours would have been. 70% in 1/100th of the time wins every time in a spreadsheet.

choices.title: Refine the AI output, salvage what you can
choices.body: You take the generated work and add the 30% the machine can't do. The result is better than either alone. Your PM doesn't notice the difference. You do.

choices.title: Fight for your original direction
choices.body: You present your work alongside the AI version. Yours is better. The timeline for yours is three weeks longer. The spreadsheet wins.

choices.title: Walk away from the project, protect your energy
choices.body: You hand it off and move to the next thing. The grief is quiet and recurring. Design is now a thing that happens to you.

title: The Design Department Is an API
body: Your company cancels the design department's budget and subscribes to a design API instead. $3k/month for unlimited AI-generated designs, reviewed by a single human overseas. Your annual salary was $140k. The API is $36k/year. The math is not on your side. The quality gap is closing while the price gap widens.

choices.title: Offer to be the human reviewer at a reduced rate
choices.body: You negotiate a contract: $60k/year to quality-check AI output. It's 57% of your old salary. The work is soul-crushing and stable.

choices.title: Leave and find a company that still values design
choices.body: The list gets shorter every quarter. You find one in healthcare. The interfaces are ugly and important. The salary is 80% of your old one.

choices.title: Start your own design practice, bet on yourself
choices.body: You go independent. The first three months are terrifying. Month four, a luxury brand finds you. They want human. They'll pay for human.

title: Newsletter Burnout
body: Six months of weekly publishing on top of your full-time job. Open rate: 42%. Your sanity rate is lower. Every Sunday you stare at a blank draft and wonder if anyone would notice if you stopped. Your sprint starts Monday.

choices.title: Switch to biweekly, protect the spark
choices.body: Three people unsubscribe. Everyone else says "honestly, same." Your weekends return.

choices.title: Hire an editor, scale properly
choices.body: The quality goes up. The cost goes up. The Sunday dread goes down.

choices.title: Shut it down, good run
choices.body: You write a final edition. The replies are kind. Your Sundays are yours again.

title: The Mentee Surpasses You
body: The junior you mentored just got promoted to your level. She credits you in her promo doc. She's better than you expected. Maybe better than you. The team is growing around you while you stay in place.

choices.title: Celebrate genuinely, suggest collaborating
choices.body: You send champagne and a DM. She agrees. You partner on the next big feature.

choices.title: Feel the sting, use it as fuel
choices.body: Proud and jealous simultaneously. You channel both into your own promo packet.

choices.title: Step back from mentoring entirely
choices.body: You've been giving away your edge. The relationship cools.

title: The Slop Reckoning
body: Your manager pulls you aside: "The last three features felt... thin." You know why. You've been leaning on AI too hard. The output is faster but it all looks the same. The design system is becoming a design prison.

choices.title: Go back to basics, rebuild from scratch
choices.body: You delete your AI templates and start from a blank artboard. The next feature takes twice as long and is twice as good.

choices.title: Refine your AI workflow, add a craft pass
choices.body: You keep the pipeline but add a human finishing step. The quality recovers.

choices.title: Lean into speed, own the volume play
choices.body: You optimize for throughput. More features ship. The design org measures output, not craft.

title: The Side Project Collapses
body: Your Figma plugin revenue dropped 80%. A competitor released an AI-generated version that's free. Passive income was never passive. It was deferred grief with a Stripe dashboard.

choices.title: Rebuild with differentiation
choices.body: You redesign with custom features AI can't replicate. Sales recover slowly.

choices.title: Shut it down, focus on the day job
choices.body: You archive the product page. Side projects aren't for everyone.

choices.title: Pivot to workshops and cohort teaching
choices.body: AI can't replicate a Zoom call with a real human. Yet.

title: The Sellout Reckoning
body: A designer friend sees the product you've been working on. "This isn't you," they text. They're right. The product is a dark-pattern subscription trap with confusing cancellation flows.

choices.title: Own it, the salary pays rent
choices.body: You reply: "Rent doesn't care about my values." They understand. Mostly.

choices.title: Push back internally, try to fix the patterns
choices.body: You write a UX ethics brief. The PM reads it. Nothing changes. But you tried.

choices.title: Finish the quarter, start job hunting
choices.body: You complete your commitments and update your LinkedIn. Moral accounting has a timeline.

title: Monetizing the Following
body: You have 8k followers. A course platform approaches: teach a masterclass on product design, 50/50 split. The money could be real. Your employer might notice.

choices.title: Record the course, go all in
choices.body: First month revenue: $7k. You become a creator against your will. HR asks about the moonlighting clause.

choices.title: Negotiate a better split, 70/30
choices.body: They counter at 60/40. The extra 10% matters when it sells for years.

choices.title: Decline, keep the following organic
choices.body: You launch a free YouTube series instead. No legal gray areas.

title: The AI Purists Come For You
