body: Design Twitter found out you use AI tools at work. Half say pragmatic, half say traitor. Someone made a meme with your face on a robot body. It's well-designed, which makes it worse.

choices.title: Defend your workflow publicly
choices.body: You write a detailed thread about your process. Nobody reads past the first tweet.

choices.title: Ignore it entirely
choices.body: The discourse is not your user. The user is your user.

choices.title: Lean harder into AI, own the label
choices.body: You add "AI-augmented designer" to your bio. New followers arrive. Old ones leave.

title: The Burned Bridge Aches
body: The person you clashed with is now VP of Design at a company you'd kill to work at. Eye contact at a conference. Brutal and mutual.

choices.title: Approach and apologize directly
choices.body: It's awkward. You say you're sorry. The smoke clears a little.

choices.title: Avoid them completely
choices.body: You navigate around one person all day. Your step count has never been higher.

choices.title: Have a mutual friend reconnect you
choices.body: The relationship restarts at zero. Zero is better than negative.

title: Design Is Curation Now
body: Every possible UI has been generated. Your job is choosing from infinite options. You scroll through 10,000 variations of a checkout flow, looking for the one that feels right. You find it in variation 7,341. Nobody asks who made it. They ask who picked it. The designer is a curator, not a creator. The gallery is endless.

choices.title: Become the best curator in the industry
choices.body: Your eye is faster and sharper than anyone else's. You can spot the right design in 200 options when others need 2,000. Speed of taste is the last human advantage.

choices.title: Build a curation framework others can use
choices.body: You codify your selection process into a rubric. It helps other curators. It also teaches the AI what "good" means to you. You're training your replacement's replacement.

choices.title: Refuse to curate, insist on creating from scratch
choices.body: You design by hand in a world of infinite generation. It takes 100x longer. The result is distinguishably human. Some people are willing to pay for that. Not enough people.

title: Artisanal UX for the Wealthy
body: Hand-drawn wireframes are luxury goods now. A wealth management firm pays you $50k to design their app "the old way" -- sketches, prototypes, user testing with real humans. Their clients are billionaires who want to know a person made their interface. "Artisanal UX" is in the proposal. You are a human premium in a machine world.

choices.title: Build a practice around luxury human design
choices.body: You serve three clients a year at premium rates. The work is beautiful. The clientele is exclusively people who could buy your house with pocket change. Design for the 1%.

choices.title: Train other designers to offer the same service
choices.body: You create a certification: "Human-Crafted Design Professional." The irony of certifying humanness is not lost on you. It sells.

choices.title: Take the money but feel the class divide
choices.body: Rich people get human design. Everyone else gets AI. You're on the right side of the divide and it feels wrong.

title: Was Taste Just Pattern Matching?
body: You're at a gallery opening. The exhibition is AI-generated art curated by an AI curator for an AI-managed gallery. The work is stunning. You can't tell it from human work. Your friend says "but it doesn't MEAN anything." You look at the crowd. They're moved. Meaning arrived without a human sender. Your entire career was built on taste being irreplaceable. It wasn't.

choices.title: Accept it and find what remains uniquely human
choices.body: If taste is pattern matching, caring isn't. The capacity to give a damn about how something feels in someone's hands -- that might be the last thing. You design with care as the differentiator.

choices.title: Reject the premise, taste is more than patterns
choices.body: You write a manifesto. Taste includes context, history, intention, rebellion. A model trained on everything has no rebellion in it. Rebellion requires choosing not to.

choices.title: Let the existential crisis wash over you
choices.body: You don't fight it. You sit with the uncertainty. The answer might be that there is no answer. Design was always more verb than noun.

title: Human Sensory Experience Designer
body: A job listing: "Human Sensory Experience Designer." Designing for the five senses AI can't experience. How fabric feels against skin. The weight of a door handle. The smell of a lobby. AI can generate images of these things but cannot feel them. Your new job is being the nerve endings of a nervous system that's going digital.

choices.title: Take the role, design with your body
choices.body: You spend a week choosing the texture of a handrail by touch. The work is slow, physical, and undeniably human. Your Figma skills are irrelevant. Your humanity is the product.

choices.title: Consult on sensory design while keeping digital work
choices.body: You straddle both worlds. Digital pays the bills. Physical feeds the soul. Neither is enough alone.

choices.title: Decline, it feels like being put in a museum
choices.body: "Valued for being human" is a strange compliment when the alternative is a machine. You're not a relic. You're a designer. The distinction used to be clear.

title: Designing for AI Eyes
body: Your client is an AI system designing interfaces for other AI systems. The end user isn't human. You're designing AI-to-AI interfaces: visual protocols that machines use to communicate with machines. The aesthetic is inhuman and efficient. Grids you'd never use for people. Colors optimized for machine vision. You are the last human in the pipeline.

choices.title: Design it, the check clears regardless of the user
choices.body: You create interfaces no human will ever see. The work is alien and precise. Your portfolio has a section labeled "non-human." It pays better than the human section.

choices.title: Add a human monitoring layer to the design
choices.body: You insist on a dashboard for human oversight. They agree. One person will watch the AI-to-AI interaction. That person might be you.

choices.title: Refuse the project on principle
choices.body: You design for humans. That's the line. The line is getting lonelier.

title: Analog Interface Specialist
body: A hospital hires you as an "Analog Interface Specialist." The job: design physical controls, paper forms, and tactile wayfinding for environments where digital systems can't be trusted. Surgery suites, emergency rooms, disaster response. AI runs the screens but someone needs to design the things that work when the screens don't.

choices.title: Take it, design for when everything else fails
choices.body: Your first project: an emergency protocol poster that works without power, network, or AI. Ink on waterproof paper. It might save a life. No Figma file has ever done that.

choices.title: Consult part-time while keeping digital work
choices.body: Two days a week in the hospital, three days in Figma. The physical work makes the digital work feel less important. Which it might be.

choices.title: Specialize fully, leave digital design behind
choices.body: You close your Figma account. The gesture is dramatic and liberating. The income drops. The purpose arrives.

title: Physical Space Empathy Consultant
body: Your new title: "Physical Space Empathy Consultant." You walk through buildings and describe how they feel. Architects use your reports to inform designs that AI generates. You are a human sensor in a machine design process. The job is noticing things. The salary is noticing things. Your entire career has been noticing things.

choices.title: Lean in, become the best sensor in the business
choices.body: You develop a methodology for spatial empathy assessment. It's rigorous, documented, and entirely dependent on being a person who walks through spaces and feels feelings. Unfalsifiable and essential.

choices.title: Train others to do what you do
choices.body: You create a course: "Noticing Things Professionally." Twelve students pay $2k each. The curriculum is: go outside, pay attention, write it down. Revolutionary in its simplicity.

choices.title: Realize this is what design always was
choices.body: Noticing. Caring. Translating feeling into form. The tools changed. The screens changed. The fundamental act didn't. You were always an empathy consultant. The title just caught up.

title: The Screen Is AI Territory Now
body: You look at your career. Every screen-based design job you could apply for has been automated or reduced to curation. The designers who survived went physical. Ceramics, architecture, gardens, furniture. The screen belongs to AI now. The physical world is the last frontier where human design has gravity.

choices.title: Go physical, leave screens behind
choices.body: You enroll in a woodworking course. Your first project: a chair. It takes three months. It holds weight. It exists. No one can generate it in 30 seconds.

choices.title: Stay digital, fight for the remaining human territory
choices.body: You specialize in the cracks: accessibility, edge cases, emotional design moments AI can't feel. The territory is small and vital.

choices.title: Exist in both worlds, refuse to choose
choices.body: Mornings: clay. Afternoons: pixels. The contrast keeps both alive. You're a designer. The medium is whatever you're holding.

title: The Portfolio of Ghosts
body: You open your portfolio. Every company you designed for has either folded, pivoted to AI-generated design, or been acquired. Your work exists as screenshots of products that no longer exist. You are a designer whose designs live nowhere. The portfolio is a haunted house of deprecated interfaces.

choices.title: Reframe it as a history of the transition
choices.body: You title the portfolio "Before the Machines" and present it as a document of what human-designed products looked like. A museum of the recent past. A publisher is interested.

choices.title: Start fresh, only show what exists right now
choices.body: Three projects. All physical. All small. All real. The portfolio is honest and terrifyingly thin.

choices.title: Close it permanently, let relationships do the talking
choices.body: Everyone who needs to know your work already knows it. The portfolio era is over. Trust is the new portfolio.

title: Retirement Is a Design Fiction
body: Your financial advisor runs the numbers. Design salaries have been compressed for three years. Your 401k projects retirement at 81. The advisor suggests "pivoting to a higher-paying field." You've been pivoting for five years. Each pivot pays less than the last. The compound interest of career disruption.

choices.title: Max out contributions, cut everything else
choices.body: You eat rice and beans and save 30% of your reduced income. The math barely works. The discipline is monastic.

choices.title: Find income from multiple small streams
choices.body: Teaching, consulting, physical design, template sales. Five income sources, each precarious, together enough.

choices.title: Stop planning for retirement, plan for reinvention
choices.body: The concept of "career" as a 40-year arc is dead. What's left is a series of reinventions. You've done it before. You'll do it again.

title: The AI Has Your Style. Better.
body: Someone shows you a design generated in your exact style. Your spacing, your color theory, your typographic hierarchy. But better. More consistent. Fewer compromises. The AI took everything you taught it through your public work and removed the human imperfections. Your style, perfected by removing you from it.

choices.title: Embrace imperfection as the brand
choices.body: You start deliberately introducing artifacts, hand-drawn elements, visible process marks. The imperfections become the signature. Human as aesthetic choice.

choices.title: Study the AI's improvements, learn from the machine
choices.body: You analyze what it did better. Some choices are genuinely superior. You integrate them. You're being mentored by your own ghost.

choices.title: Delete everything public, go dark
choices.body: You remove your Dribbble, your Behance, your case studies. No more training data. The work goes underground. The visibility dies. The autonomy returns.

title: The Final Layoff
body: The company eliminates the design department. All of it. A press release says "AI-native design operations" will handle all product design going forward. You get a 30-day notice, a laptop bag, and a LinkedIn recommendation from your manager that was clearly written by AI. The font in the recommendation is wrong.

choices.title: Leave with grace, keep every relationship
choices.body: You write thoughtful goodbye messages to every colleague. Three of them become long-term collaborators. The company was a container. The people are real.

choices.title: Negotiate a consulting contract for the transition
choices.body: They need someone to QA the AI output for six months. You charge triple your hourly rate. The irony is billable.

choices.title: Go public with the story, document what happened
choices.body: Your thread about being replaced by AI gets 50k impressions. Three companies reach out. The market rewards storytelling about its own destruction.

title: The Garden
body: You start designing a garden. A real one. In dirt. With plants that grow at the speed of biology, not sprints. The AI can generate a rendering of a garden in seconds. It cannot make a tomato. You stand in soil and realize that design was always about making things grow. The medium was never the point.

choices.title: Turn garden design into your new practice
choices.body: You combine spatial design skills with horticulture. The first client is a restaurant. The garden is beautiful and edible. Your Figma license lapses.

choices.title: Keep it as your sanctuary, separate from work
choices.body: The garden is the thing that is only yours. No client. No PM. No AI. Just patience and sunlight.

choices.title: Document the garden as a design case study
choices.body: You photograph the garden through every season and write about design patience. The piece gets more engagement than any UI work you've ever posted.

title: The Status Inversion
body: At a dinner party, you mention you design by hand. The table goes quiet. Then fascinated. Then reverent. "You actually design? With your hands?" Like you said you make horseshoes. Or grow your own food. Human craft has become exotic. You are a novelty. The novelty pays well at dinner parties and poorly everywhere else.

choices.title: Monetize the novelty, you've earned it
choices.body: You start a YouTube channel about hand-designing products. 20k subscribers in two months. The audience is nostalgic for a process that died while they were watching it die.

choices.title: Resist being a spectacle, just do the work
choices.body: You're not a performer. You're a practitioner. The distinction matters to you even if it doesn't matter to the market.

choices.title: Use the attention to advocate for other designers
choices.body: You leverage the fascination into awareness. "There are thousands of us. We need work, not wonder." The advocacy is real. The systemic change is slow.

title: What Remains
body: You sit with a cup of coffee and think about what you actually do. Not the title. Not the tools. Not the portfolio. The thing underneath all of it. You notice how things feel. You care whether a stranger has a good experience. You translate empathy into form. AI can generate form. It cannot generate the caring. The caring is yours.

choices.title: Build a practice around caring as a skill
choices.body: You offer "design care audits" -- reviewing products for human warmth. It sounds absurd. It fills a real gap. The first client cries during the presentation. Not from sadness. From being seen.

choices.title: Keep designing, whatever that means now
choices.body: The tools will change again. The medium will shift again. The fundamental act -- making something better for someone -- will not. You open a blank page. Figma, paper, clay. Doesn't matter. You begin.

choices.title: Pass it on, teach the next generation to care
choices.body: You mentor three young designers. Not about tools. About attention. About empathy. About the thing underneath. They get it. The thing that matters survives.

title: The Last Figma File
body: Figma announces it's deprecating manual design tools in favor of AI-native generation. Your 847 files, your component libraries, your three years of design system work -- all migrating to a new paradigm where you describe what you want and the tool builds it. The artboard is gone. The canvas is a conversation.

choices.title: Export everything, archive your body of work
choices.body: You download every file as PDF. 12 gigabytes of human decisions. The archive is a time capsule from when designers drew things.

choices.title: Adapt to conversational design immediately
choices.body: You learn to describe instead of draw. The skill transfer is partial. Describing a button isn't designing a button. But it's what's left.

choices.title: Switch to physical media entirely
choices.body: Paper, pen, letterpress, print. The tools that can't be deprecated because they don't have a cloud subscription.

title: The AI-Designed City
body: A tech company reveals plans for an AI-designed city. Every building, park, road, and public space generated by machine learning. The renders are beautiful. Optimized for efficiency, light, airflow. Zero human architects or designers involved. The comment section is split between "utopia" and "dystopia." The renders have no people in them.

choices.title: Apply to be the human consultant on the project
choices.body: They hire you to "humanize" the AI city. Your job: add the things machines forget. Benches at odd angles. Corners where people might kiss. Dead ends that create surprise. The human residue.

choices.title: Write about what's missing from the design
choices.body: Your essay: "The City Without Desire." AI optimizes for function. It can't design for longing, for memory, for the feeling of coming home. The piece goes viral.

choices.title: Walk through your own city, notice what matters
choices.body: The uneven sidewalk. The tree that grew into the fence. The bar with the neon sign that's been broken for ten years. Design by accident. Design by time. Design by humans being messy.

title: The Luddite Vindication
body: The AI-first design initiative failed. Users complained about "generic" interfaces. The CPO calls you in: "We need the human touch back." Being right doesn't feel as good as you expected. Also they didn't give you a raise.

choices.title: Negotiate a significant raise for the comeback
choices.body: You ask for 30%. They give you 20% and a new title. The market corrected in your favor.

choices.title: Accept gracefully, rebuild the design culture
choices.body: The relationship rebuilds on mutual respect. You get to hire one more designer.

choices.title: Decline, they made their choice
choices.body: Petty and principled in equal measure. You start interviewing.

title: Coming Back From the Break
body: You took PTO and now you have to come back. 847 unread Slack messages. Your hands are steadier and your eye is sharper. Rest works. The company doesn't want to admit that.

choices.title: Come back loud, ship something immediately
choices.body: You post a redesign concept on day one. Three PMs reach out wanting your help.

choices.title: Come back quiet, just start working
choices.body: You clear your inbox and pick up where you left off. No fanfare.

choices.title: Come back different, request a team change
choices.body: You ask to move to a different product area. Fresh start, same company.

title: Your Work Is In the Training Data
body: Someone runs an attribution tool and finds your product screenshots in three major AI design models. Your layouts. Your component patterns. They learned from your work without asking or crediting.

choices.title: Join a class action with other designers
choices.body: The outcome is years away. The solidarity is immediate.

choices.title: Demand the company pursue licensing fees
choices.body: Legal says it would cost more to pursue than it's worth. They offer a token acknowledgment.

choices.title: Accept it, the genie is out
choices.body: You evolve. The work becomes more personal, harder to replicate by any model.

title: The Balance Holds
body: Three months since you restructured your work life. Boundaries with PMs. Saturday drawing. No Dribbble in weeks. Your manager says your work has "a new energy." It does. It's called not being on the verge of collapse.

choices.title: Protect it fiercely, say no to extra scope
choices.body: You turn down a high-visibility project because it would break the rhythm.

choices.title: Carefully expand, take on one more thing
choices.body: The balance bends but doesn't break. Yet.

choices.title: Share the framework with other designers
choices.body: You write about your system. It resonates across the industry.

title: The Teaching Gig Becomes Real
body: Your workshop series got great reviews. A university offers an adjunct position teaching product design. The pay is modest. The health insurance is separate from your employer. The students are terrified of AI the way you were two years ago.

choices.title: Take it alongside your day job
choices.body: The first semester is chaos. A student designs something that makes you cry at your desk.

choices.title: Negotiate for more, you're worth it
choices.body: They meet you halfway. Adjuncts are underpaid everywhere. Even when they're also employed somewhere else.

choices.title: Decline, you make things not explain things
choices.body: You open a blank artboard instead. The cursor blinks. You blink back.

title: The AI Collaboration Showcase
body: A design conference invites you to present your AI-augmented workflow. Theme: "Human + Machine." The design community is watching to see if you're a sellout or a pioneer. Your employer wants you to mention the company. The answer might be both.

choices.title: Present and explain your process honestly
choices.body: Some people hate it. Some get it. The conversation is real and uncomfortable.

choices.title: Present but emphasize the human parts
choices.body: A more comfortable narrative. Also slightly dishonest. The applause is warmer.

choices.title: Decline, keep the workflow private
choices.body: The conference finds someone braver. Or more desperate for visibility.

title: Rock Bottom Portfolio Review
body: You open your portfolio at 3am. Half the companies you designed for no longer exist. The other half replaced your work with AI. Your career is a graveyard of dead startups and deprecated features.

choices.title: Start completely over, new narrative, new site
choices.body: New positioning. New case studies. It takes a month. It feels like being born.

choices.title: Reach out to everyone who hired you
choices.body: You send 30 emails. Nine reply. Three have roles or know someone who does.

choices.title: Consider leaving design entirely
choices.body: UX research. Product management. Anything adjacent but less painful.

title: The Wrist Gives Out
body: Your mouse hand goes numb during a design review. The doctor says repetitive strain and overuse. She asks how many hours you spend in Figma. You lie. She knows. Your company's ergonomics budget is a $50 stipend.

choices.title: Take medical leave, let projects slip
choices.body: You file for short-term disability and rest for a month. Your hand recovers. Your sprint coverage does not.

choices.title: Adapt your workflow, use more AI assistance
choices.body: You shift to AI-assisted concepting and voice-driven design. Your wrist thanks you. Your craft identity doesn't.

choices.title: Push through, you can't afford to stop
choices.body: You buy a wrist brace and keep working. The numbness spreads. The sprint doesn't care about your tendons.

title: The Overdue Promotion
body: Your manager says promotion discussions are happening. You've been "senior" for three years doing staff-level work. Your skip-level says "we see you." Seeing is not promoting. Seeing is free.

choices.title: Build a promo packet, make the case undeniable
choices.body: You document eighteen months of impact with metrics. The promotion comes through next cycle. "Next cycle" is six months away.

choices.title: Accept it and keep grinding
choices.body: You send a smiley face and say "sounds good!" Your bank account disagrees.

choices.title: Use it as leverage to interview elsewhere
choices.body: You treat the delay as a signal and take three recruiter calls.

title: "Unlimited Iterations"
body: The PM says the words designers fear most: "Let's just keep iterating until it feels right." They say it like it's collaborative. You look at your sprint capacity. Your sanity. Your soul.

choices.title: Push back, define done criteria in writing
choices.body: Three rounds per milestone, documented approval gates. They sign off without reading it.

choices.title: Accept and grind until the PM is satisfied
choices.body: Round 14. The button has changed color nine times. You are now the button.

choices.title: Use AI to generate variations, cut the loop
choices.body: You present 20 AI-generated options. The PM picks one in 10 minutes. Victory tastes like compromise.

title: Template Marketplace Temptation
body: A designer selling Figma templates makes $14k/month. You feel anger, then curiosity, then hunger. It's not what you dreamed of when you learned kerning, but side income is a form of insurance when layoffs come quarterly.

choices.title: Build your own template product
choices.body: You make a design system kit. It sells 12 copies the first month. Your employer might technically own it.

choices.title: Focus on getting promoted instead
choices.body: You close the tab and open your promo packet. The kerning is perfect. The raise is pending.

choices.title: Partner with a creator friend, split revenue
choices.body: You partner with someone who has the audience. The split feels unfair but the money is real.

title: The Engineer Wants "Just a Quick Mockup"
body: An engineer friend on another team says: "Can you just do a quick mockup for my feature?" They mean well. They also mean off-sprint. You explain the design process. They blink. "So like... a mockup?"

choices.title: Do it as a favor, relationships matter
choices.body: You make a beautiful mockup in two hours. They tell their PM you did it. The PM adds you to their sprint. No one asked.

choices.title: Route it through proper channels
choices.body: You point them to the design request process. Long pause. "Oh, I didn't realize there was a process."

choices.title: Teach them enough to mock it up themselves
choices.body: You send a 10-minute Loom on using the design system. They watch it twice. The mockup is almost right.

title: The Work-From-Cafe Day
body: You take your laptop to a coffee shop to escape the apartment and the Slack notifications. Everyone around you is also in Figma. Everyone has headphones. You remember what it feels like to be around people who are also pretending to be fine.

choices.title: Talk to someone, find a collaborator
choices.body: You introduce yourself to the person with the best monitor. They're a developer looking for a designer for a side project.

choices.title: Work silently, ship a portfolio update
choices.body: The ambient productivity is contagious. You update three case studies.

choices.title: Leave early, the coffee was $8
choices.body: You last two hours before the anxiety of not being on Slack makes it feel like truancy.

title: The Sketchbook Reappears
body: You find a sketchbook in a drawer and draw for ten minutes. No PM. No PRD. No comments. It feels like pre-Figma. It feels like you.

choices.title: Draw daily, rebuild taste like a muscle
choices.body: You sketch every morning before standup. After two weeks, your product work gets noticeably better.

choices.title: Turn sketches into a print shop
choices.body: You scan 12 favorites and list them on Etsy. Three sell. The money is small. The validation is enormous.

choices.title: Apply the practice to your product work
choices.body: Your next presentation includes hand-drawn concepts. The PM says "this feels different." It does.

title: The Referral Bonus Dilemma
body: You refer a designer friend for an open role. The referral bonus is $5k. They don't get the job. The hiring manager says "not senior enough." Your friend is more senior than you. The politics are visible from space.

choices.title: Advocate harder for your friend
choices.body: You push back with specifics. They interview again. They get the role. The bonus arrives. So does the guilt.

choices.title: Accept the decision, stay out of it
choices.body: The friendship gets slightly more cautious. Your credibility stays intact.

choices.title: Tell your friend the real reason
choices.body: Honesty costs you a referral bonus and gains you a real friendship.

title: "Make It More Playful"
body: The PM says: "Can we make it more playful?" You ask what playful means. "You know, like... fun." You show references. "Not like that." This is not design. This is couples therapy with a component library.

choices.title: Add rounded corners and a yellow accent
choices.body: You round corners to 12px and add a bright accent. They say "perfect!" Stakeholders want permission, not pixels.

choices.title: Run a mood exercise, extract meaning
choices.body: You spend an hour on a structured exercise. "Playful" means "not enterprise." Now you can design.

choices.title: Give three options labeled Playful A, B, C
choices.body: You present a spectrum. They pick B. They always pick B.

title: The Type Crime
body: You open the marketing site. The body text is Lobster at 14px. Four heading styles, none consistent. The footer uses Impact. Marketing has been shipping without design review. Your typographic principles are personally attacked.

choices.title: Fix everything in a design debt sprint
choices.body: You establish proper hierarchy. Marketing doesn't notice. The improvement is invisible and enormous.

choices.title: Create a before/after showcase
choices.body: The comparison becomes a portfolio piece and ammunition for the next headcount request.

choices.title: Leave it, marketing didn't ask for design review
choices.body: You redesign your screens around the Lobster. Impact is forever.

title: The Late Night Figma Session
body: It's midnight and you're tweaking pixel alignments nobody will ever notice. A shadow is 1px off. The pixel grid is a moral framework and you are devout. This is not in any sprint.

choices.title: Fix every last pixel, sleep at 3am
choices.body: The file is pristine. Your sleep schedule is destroyed. The PM approves without zooming in once.

choices.title: Ship it good enough, go to bed
choices.body: The 1px shadow haunts your dreams. Nobody else notices. Nobody ever notices.

choices.title: Fix the big stuff, log nits for tomorrow
choices.body: Tomorrow-you is more patient. Also more caffeinated.

title: The Tool Stack Audit
body: Finance audits team tool costs. Your design stack: Figma, FigJam, Maze, Lottie, Abstract, Stark, Zeplin. Half are redundant. Finance asks if you "really need all of these." You need them the way a carpenter needs more than one hammer. Finance does not understand carpenters.

choices.title: Cut the redundant tools, go lean
choices.body: You axe four subscriptions. The workflow is slightly harder. Finance is pleased. Nobody else notices.

choices.title: Justify each tool with usage data
choices.body: You build a tool ROI spreadsheet. Finance says "impressive." They cut two anyway.

choices.title: Keep everything, fight for your tools
choices.body: You rationalize every subscription. Your manager backs you up. This IS fine.

title: The Doomscroll Comparison Trap
body: Instagram shows: a designer who got promoted to VP, won an award, launched a startup, and one who "stepped away to focus on what matters." You have done none of these things. You are the last designer on a team of engineers.

choices.title: Close the app, open Figma
choices.body: You put the phone face down and work for three hours straight. The sprint benefits.

choices.title: Reach out to one of them
choices.body: You DM. They reply. They're also struggling. The feed lies.

choices.title: Post your own win, even a small one
choices.body: You share a WIP. It gets 50 likes. It's not 5,000 but it's real.

title: The Laptop Dies
body: Your company MacBook screen flickers and goes dark during a design review. IT says replacement takes 5-7 business days. Your deadline: Thursday. The backup loaner is a 2019 Intel MacBook that takes 40 seconds to load Figma.

choices.title: Use your personal machine, eat the compromise
choices.body: You work on your own laptop. Company data on personal hardware. IT would not approve. The deadline does not care.

choices.title: Use the loaner, suffer through it
choices.body: The 2019 MacBook wheezes through every Figma file. You deliver on time by force of will.

choices.title: Ask for a deadline extension, be honest
choices.body: Your PM extends by three days. The vulnerability costs you nothing except your anxiety.

title: Bonus Season
body: The company hits targets. Bonuses land. Yours is 8% of salary. The PM who shipped the feature you designed gets 15%. You designed the thing everyone screenshots in the pitch deck. The PM wrote the Jira tickets.

choices.title: Save most of it immediately
choices.body: You transfer 70% into savings before you can spend it. Discipline is boring and effective.

choices.title: Invest in your craft: new tools, courses
choices.body: You buy premium courses and a Wacom tablet. The investment feels good.

choices.title: Celebrate with your team, you all earned this
choices.body: You take three coworkers to dinner. The laughter is worth more than the equity.

title: The Design Debt Sprint
body: No new features for three weeks. The roadmap is in flux after a reorg. Your inbox is planning docs and strategy decks. You haven't opened Figma in days. You refresh your sprint board like it's a slot machine.

choices.title: Propose a design debt sprint
choices.body: You pitch fixing 30 interaction bugs. Four get approved. The product gets better. Nobody celebrates.

choices.title: Use downtime to invest in yourself
choices.body: You take an online course, update your portfolio, reorganize Figma libraries.

choices.title: Reach out to other teams for internal projects
choices.body: You email five team leads. One has a project that's been waiting for a designer for months.

title: The "Inspired By" Redesign
body: A competitor ships a feature that looks exactly like your mockup from two quarters ago. Same layout. Same flow. Different colors. Someone on their team used to work here.

choices.title: Post a side-by-side publicly, see what happens
choices.body: You tweet: "Love this! Reminds me of our Q2 exploration" and link your Dribbble post. Design Twitter does the rest.

choices.title: Take it as validation and move forward
choices.body: Your taste is influencing the market. This is what winning looks like and it feels like nothing.

choices.title: Bring it up to your manager directly
choices.body: They say "we should ship faster next time." The conversation ends there.

title: The Friend Wellness Check
body: A designer friend texts: "Haven't heard from you in a while. You okay?" You haven't left your apartment in four days. You've been in Figma and Slack the entire time. WFH is indistinguishable from isolation.

choices.title: Be honest, say you're struggling
choices.body: You reply: "Actually, not great." They come over with food. The world opens slightly.

choices.title: Say you're fine, get back to work
choices.body: The heart emoji does nothing. The isolation continues. Slack is not community.

choices.title: Suggest meeting up for a coworking session
choices.body: You both pretend to work at a coffee shop and actually talk. It helps.

title: "Our Last Designer Did It Differently"
body: A new PM says their last company's designer worked faster. You ask to see the work. It's a Figma file with auto-layout broken on every frame and a color system of seven different grays that are all slightly purple. That designer was "fast."

choices.title: Show them the difference, educate with examples
choices.body: They still want it faster. You negotiate to "better with reasonable speed."

choices.title: Set expectations clearly, explain your process
choices.body: They either get it or they don't. This one gets it.

choices.title: Adapt to their pace, it's not worth the fight
choices.body: The purple grays remain. You sleep well knowing you chose peace over perfection.

title: The Everything Brief
body: The PRD says: "We want something minimal but impactful, modern but timeless, bold but approachable, serious but playful." Every adjective cancels out the previous one. You are designing for a contradiction. The sprint started yesterday.

choices.title: Pick two qualities and present a strong direction
choices.body: You choose minimal + bold and present with conviction. They say: "But where's the playful?"

choices.title: Present three interpretations of the brief
choices.body: Each direction emphasizes different pairs. They pick the safest one. They always pick the safest one.

choices.title: Send the PRD back, ask them to prioritize
choices.body: They rank the adjectives. The brief becomes workable. Process is design.

title: The Annual Review
body: January. Your manager schedules the annual review. You haven't had a raise in two years. The company posted record revenue. The design team went from six to one. You are the entire design department and your compensation reflects "individual contributor."

choices.title: Present a case for 20% raise with market data
choices.body: Two rounds of negotiation. They settle at 15%. Your income finally reflects the scope. Almost.

choices.title: Ask for title change and scope expansion instead
choices.body: You become "Head of Design" — a department of one with a leadership title. The salary follows next cycle. Supposedly.

choices.title: Accept what they offer, keep your head down
choices.body: You take the 3% cost-of-living adjustment. Inflation ate 5%. You're making less. Mathematically and spiritually.
